 Chhath Puja 2026: Date, Four Days of Rituals, Story of Chhathi Maiya, Surya Arghya, Significance and Celebrations

 Chhath Puja 2026: Date and Day 
 Chhath Puja 2026 will be observed from November 13 to November 16 , with the main Chhath Puja and Sandhya Arghya taking place on Sunday, November 15. The festival concludes with Usha Arghya on Monday, November 16.
 Dedicated to the Sun God, Surya Dev, and Chhathi Maiya, Chhath is a four-day Hindu festival marked by prayers, ritual bathing, strict fasting and offerings made to the setting and rising Sun. It is particularly significant in Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Nepal, although it is now celebrated by communities across India and abroad.
 The festival is also known as Surya Shashthi, Chhathi, Dala Chhath and Pratihar. Its central rituals express gratitude to the Sun, which sustains life on Earth, and seek blessings for health, prosperity, family well-being and longevity.
 Chhath Puja 2026: Four-Day Calendar
 Day Date Day of the week Main observance 
 Day 1 November 13, 2026 Friday Nahay Khay 
 Day 2 November 14, 2026 Saturday Kharna or Lohanda 
 Day 3 November 15, 2026 Sunday Sandhya Arghya 
 Day 4 November 16, 2026 Monday Usha Arghya and Parana 
 The main Chhath observance falls on Kartik Shukla Shashthi, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik.
 Chhath Puja 2026: Tithi and Arghya Timings
 According to the Kolkata Panchang, Kartik Shukla Shashthi begins at approximately 11:23 PM on November 14 and ends at approximately 2:00 AM on November 16.
 The main offerings are made around sunset on November 15 and sunrise on November 16.
 For Kolkata:
 Sandhya Arghya: November 15, around 4:53 PM (sunset).
 Usha Arghya: November 16, around 5:50 AM (sunrise).
 These timings are location-specific. Sunset and sunrise vary across cities, so devotees should consult their local Panchang or the timings published by their local administration.
 What Is Chhath Puja? 
 Chhath Puja is a Hindu festival dedicated primarily to the worship of Surya Dev, the Sun God, and Chhathi Maiya, who is associated with Shashthi Devi in Hindu tradition.
 The word Chhath is commonly understood as a regional form of the word Shashthi, referring to the sixth lunar day on which the main observance takes place.
 Unlike festivals centred mainly on temple worship or elaborate idol ceremonies, Chhath is characterised by direct offerings to the Sun. Devotees gather at riverbanks, ponds, lakes and other water bodies to offer Arghya, a ritual offering of water and other materials.
 The festival is particularly distinctive because prayers are offered to both the setting Sun and the rising Sun. The evening offering is known as Sandhya Arghya, while the morning offering is called Usha Arghya.
 Chhath is also associated with rigorous discipline. Devotees observe dietary restrictions, maintain ritual cleanliness and, during the main fasting period, abstain from food and water.
 Why Is Chhath Puja Celebrated? 
 Chhath Puja is celebrated to express gratitude and devotion towards the Sun God, regarded in Hindu tradition as a source of light, energy, warmth and life.
 The Sun plays an essential role in sustaining life on Earth. It supports plant growth, influences seasonal cycles and provides the energy that drives many natural processes. The festival reflects the traditional recognition of this dependence on the Sun.
 Devotees observe Chhath to pray for:
 Good health and well-being.
 The longevity and prosperity of family members.
 The happiness and welfare of children.
 The fulfilment of sincere wishes.
 Peace and prosperity in the household.
 Gratitude for nature and the resources that sustain life.
 Although women are traditionally the most visible participants in many Chhath celebrations, men also observe the fast and perform the rituals. The person undertaking the Chhath fast is known as a vrati .
 Who Is Chhathi Maiya? 
 Chhathi Maiya is one of the central divine figures associated with Chhath Puja. She is traditionally identified with Shashthi Devi, a goddess associated with the protection and well-being of children.
 In Hindu religious traditions, Shashthi Devi is regarded as a protector of children and is worshipped by families seeking blessings for childbirth, child health and family welfare.
 Chhathi Maiya is particularly revered during Chhath, when devotees offer prayers alongside their worship of Surya Dev.
 The precise descriptions of Chhathi Maiya and her relationship with other divine figures can differ across regional traditions and devotional accounts. In the popular religious understanding of Chhath, she is worshipped as a motherly divine presence who blesses families and protects children.
 The Four Days of Chhath Puja: Rituals Explained 
 Chhath Puja is observed over four days, each with a distinct set of customs. Preparations, cleanliness, food restrictions and prayers form an important part of the observance.
 Day 1: Nahay Khay – November 13, 2026
 Nahay Khay marks the beginning of Chhath Puja. The name is commonly translated as “bathe and eat”.
 On this day, devotees take a ritual bath, often in a river or another water body, and prepare for the days of fasting and worship ahead. Homes and cooking spaces are thoroughly cleaned, and the food is prepared with particular attention to cleanliness and customary restrictions.
 The person observing the fast generally eats a simple, freshly prepared meal. A traditional meal in Bihar and neighbouring regions often includes:
 Rice.
 Chana dal.
 Bottle gourd, commonly called kaddu or lauki.
 Other permitted vegetables prepared according to family customs.
 Kaddu-bhat, a preparation of bottle gourd, rice and dal, is particularly associated with Nahay Khay.
 Food is commonly prepared without onion and garlic, and many families use separate utensils and cooking arrangements for Chhath preparations.
 Nahay Khay establishes the discipline and ritual purity followed throughout the festival.
 Day 2: Kharna or Lohanda – November 14, 2026
 The second day is known as Kharna or Lohanda.
 The vrati observes a fast during the day and traditionally breaks it in the evening after sunset, following the prescribed preparations and prayers.
 One of the best-known offerings prepared on Kharna is rasiao , a type of rice pudding generally made with rice, milk and jaggery. It is often accompanied by roti or other preparations made according to family tradition.
 The Kharna prasad is first offered in worship and then distributed among family members, relatives and neighbours.
 After the Kharna meal, the main period of the rigorous Chhath fast begins. Traditionally, devotees observe a nirjala vrat , meaning a fast without food or water, which continues until the morning offering on the fourth day.
 This period is commonly described as lasting approximately 36 hours, although the exact duration depends on the timing of the Kharna meal and the morning Parana.
 Day 3: Sandhya Arghya – November 15, 2026
 The third day is the main day of Chhath Puja and is known as Sandhya Arghya.
 Devotees prepare the offerings and arrange them in traditional bamboo baskets and winnowing trays. Family members carry these baskets to riverbanks, ponds, lakes and designated Chhath ghats.
 As sunset approaches, devotees enter the water, often standing in it, and offer Arghya to the setting Sun.
 The offerings may include fruits, sugarcane, thekua, rice preparations, coconuts and other traditional items.
 The setting Sun receives particular reverence during this ceremony. The ritual is an expression of gratitude for the Sun’s role in sustaining life and an important part of Chhath’s distinctive worship practices.
 Families and communities gather at the ghats, where traditional Chhath songs are sung. The atmosphere is often accompanied by devotional music, prayers and the illumination of earthen lamps.
 Kosi Ritual
 In several communities, a special ceremony known as Kosi is performed on the evening of Sandhya Arghya.
 A structure is traditionally prepared using sugarcane sticks, often arranged like a small canopy. Earthen lamps are placed around or beneath it, and offerings are arranged as part of the ceremony.
 The ritual may be performed at home or at the ghat, depending on local customs. Its precise form and associated prayers vary between families and regions.
 Day 4: Usha Arghya and Parana – November 16, 2026
 The fourth and final day is known as Usha Arghya.
 Devotees return to the riverbank or another designated water body before sunrise. They stand in the water and offer Arghya to the rising Sun.
 This is the concluding major ritual of Chhath Puja. The morning offering is followed by prayers and blessings, after which the vrati completes the fast through Parana.
 Parana refers to the breaking of the fast. Traditionally, the vrati takes prasad after the morning worship and then eats a meal according to the family’s customs.
 Thekua and other offerings are distributed among relatives, neighbours and devotees.
 With Usha Arghya and Parana, the four-day Chhath observance comes to an end.
 Why Are Both the Setting Sun and Rising Sun Worshipped? 
 One of the most distinctive features of Chhath Puja is that devotees offer prayers to both the setting and rising Sun.
 In many forms of traditional Sun worship, the rising Sun receives particular attention because it marks the beginning of a new day. Chhath, however, also gives a central place to the setting Sun.
 The evening Sandhya Arghya expresses gratitude to the Sun as the day comes to an end. The following morning, Usha Arghya welcomes the rising Sun and offers prayers for continued life, health and prosperity.
 The two ceremonies together represent gratitude, continuity and reverence for the natural cycle of day and night.
 The practice is also popularly understood as a reminder that the setting Sun deserves the same reverence as the rising Sun.
 The Story of Chhath Puja: Traditional Accounts and Religious Associations 
 Chhath Puja is associated with several traditional accounts involving Surya Dev, Chhathi Maiya and figures from Hindu sacred narratives. These stories are remembered through regional oral traditions, devotional songs and religious retellings.
 There is no single universally accepted historical account establishing the exact origin of the festival. The following are among the best-known traditional stories associated with Chhath.
 1. Karna and the Worship of the Sun God
 One popular traditional account connects Chhath’s Sun worship with Karna, a central character in the Mahabharata.
 Karna was the son of Surya Dev and Kunti. According to the epic tradition, he was known for his generosity, courage and devotion to his divine father.
 Karna is popularly remembered as a devoted worshipper of the Sun. Some regional accounts associate his daily prayers and offerings to Surya with the tradition of Chhath worship.
 The story is particularly significant because Karna’s relationship with Surya Dev is an important part of his identity in the Mahabharata.
 However, the claim that Karna established the present-day four-day Chhath festival is a popular traditional association rather than a conclusively documented historical fact.
 2. Draupadi and the Pandavas
 Another popular account links Chhath-related worship with Draupadi and the Pandavas.
 According to devotional retellings, Draupadi and the Pandavas faced difficulties during their period of hardship. In one version of the account, they sought divine blessings through the worship of Surya Dev.
 The story associates Sun worship with the hope of overcoming difficulties and restoring prosperity.
 Different regional versions recount the details differently, and the story is remembered as part of the wider devotional tradition surrounding Chhath.
 3. Lord Rama and Goddess Sita
 Some traditions also connect Chhath with Lord Rama and Goddess Sita.
 According to one popular account, after returning to Ayodhya from their period of exile, Rama and Sita performed a Sun-worship ritual during the month of Kartik.
 This account is sometimes cited as an explanation for the festival’s association with the Kartik period.
 The story is part of the religious narratives associated with Chhath, although its details and interpretation vary across retellings.
 4. Chhathi Maiya and the Protection of Children
 Chhath is also connected with the worship of Shashthi Devi, popularly known as Chhathi Maiya.
 In Hindu traditions, Shashthi Devi is associated with childbirth, the protection of children and family welfare. Her worship is therefore particularly meaningful to devotees who pray for the health and happiness of their children.
 This association helps explain why Chhath is often observed with prayers for children and the well-being of the entire family.
 Why Is Chhath Puja Considered One of the Most Difficult Hindu Fasts? 
 Chhath is widely regarded as one of the most demanding traditional Hindu observances because of its strict fasting rules and extended period of ritual discipline.
 The main fast generally begins after the Kharna meal on the second day and continues until Parana following Usha Arghya on the fourth day.
 During this period, the vrati traditionally abstains from both food and water. Devotees also follow specific rules concerning cleanliness, cooking, prayer and the preparation of offerings.
 The observance requires considerable preparation and is supported by family members, who help arrange food, baskets, transport and other ceremonial requirements.
 The fasting practice is a religious vow and should not be treated as a general health or wellness recommendation. Anyone with a medical condition, pregnancy or other health-related concerns should seek appropriate medical guidance before attempting a prolonged fast.
 Chhath Puja Samagri: Items Required for the Ritual 
 The materials used during Chhath Puja are largely traditional, locally sourced offerings and household items.
 A typical Chhath preparation may include:
 Bamboo baskets, known as daura and soop.
 Sugarcane.
 Thekua.
 Rice laddoos or other traditional rice preparations.
 Bananas.
 Coconuts.
 Apples and other seasonal fruits.
 Lemons.
 Ginger.
 Turmeric.
 Radish.
 Sweet potatoes.
 Jaggery.
 Rice.
 Wheat flour.
 Earthen lamps or diyas.
 Flowers.
 A vessel for offering water to the Sun.
 The exact list differs according to regional customs, family traditions and the particular ritual being performed.
 Why Are Bamboo Baskets Used?
 Bamboo baskets and winnowing trays are an important part of Chhath’s visual and ceremonial identity.
 The offerings are arranged in these baskets and carried to the ghats. The soop is a traditional winnowing tray, while daura commonly refers to a larger basket used for carrying the offerings.
 These items are often prepared or purchased from local artisans, making bamboo craft an important part of the festival economy.
 Thekua: The Most Famous Chhath Prasad 
 Thekua is one of the most recognisable offerings associated with Chhath Puja, particularly in Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
 It is a traditional sweet preparation made primarily from wheat flour and jaggery or sugar. Ghee is commonly used, and some recipes include coconut, fennel seeds or cardamom for flavour.
 The ingredients are mixed into a dough, shaped into small pieces and deep-fried until they become firm and golden brown.
 Thekua is prepared as an offering to the Sun God and is later distributed among family members, relatives, neighbours and other devotees.
 Its importance goes beyond its role as a sweet. The preparation is closely associated with family participation, traditional cooking methods and the distinctive food culture of Chhath.
 Other Traditional Chhath Offerings
 Apart from thekua, several other foods and fruits are commonly included in Chhath offerings.
 Rasiao: A rice pudding prepared with milk and jaggery, particularly associated with the Kharna meal.
 Kasaar: A traditional preparation generally made using coarsely ground rice or rice flour, jaggery and ghee.
 Rice laddoos: Sweet rice-based preparations that are included in offerings in some communities.
 Seasonal fruits: Bananas, coconuts, apples, sweet limes and other fruits are commonly arranged in the offering baskets.
 Sugarcane: Sugarcane is an important offering and is also used in the Kosi ritual in several regions.
 The ingredients and recipes are not identical across all Chhath-observing communities.
 Chhath Puja in Bihar: The Festival’s Cultural Heartland 
 Bihar is one of the most important centres of Chhath Puja celebrations. The festival is deeply connected with the state’s cultural identity and is observed across urban neighbourhoods, villages and towns.
 In cities such as Patna, Gaya, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Darbhanga, large numbers of devotees gather at riverbanks and specially prepared ghats.
 The banks of the Ganga and other rivers become major centres of worship. Local authorities and community groups often arrange cleaning drives, lighting, temporary facilities and safety measures ahead of the festival.
 Families prepare for Chhath several days in advance. Markets become busy with the sale of fruits, sugarcane, bamboo baskets, earthen lamps, wheat flour and jaggery.
 Traditional folk songs form an important part of the celebrations. These songs are passed down through generations and often describe the devotion of the vrati, the importance of Surya Dev and the blessings of Chhathi Maiya.
 Chhath Puja in Patna
 Patna witnesses large-scale Chhath celebrations, particularly along the banks of the Ganga.
 Several riverfront locations and designated ghats become gathering points for devotees. Families carry their offerings to the water’s edge and participate in Sandhya Arghya and Usha Arghya.
 The festival is also marked by extensive public preparations, including ghat cleaning, lighting and crowd-management arrangements.
 Chhath Puja in Jharkhand 
 Chhath Puja is widely celebrated in Jharkhand, where devotees gather around rivers, ponds, lakes and reservoirs.
 Ranchi, Jamshedpur, Dhanbad, Bokaro and other urban centres witness community celebrations.
 The rituals remain similar to those followed in Bihar, including Nahay Khay, Kharna, Sandhya Arghya and Usha Arghya.
 Local folk songs, traditional food and family gatherings contribute to the festival’s regional character.
 Chhath Puja in Uttar Pradesh 
 Chhath is particularly popular in eastern Uttar Pradesh, including districts with strong cultural and historical connections to Bihar.
 Devotees in areas such as Varanasi, Gorakhpur, Ballia, Deoria and neighbouring regions perform the four-day rituals.
 Riverbanks and local water bodies become important centres of worship. In Varanasi, the ghats along the Ganga provide prominent locations for evening and morning offerings.
 The festival is also celebrated by migrant communities from eastern Uttar Pradesh living in major Indian cities.
 Chhath Puja in Nepal 
 Chhath Puja is also an important festival in Nepal, particularly in the Terai region, where it is observed by Hindu communities.
 Devotees perform rituals along rivers, ponds and other water bodies, offering Arghya to the setting and rising Sun.
 The festival is especially significant in areas such as Janakpur, Birgunj and other parts of the Madhesh region.
 The celebrations share many features with those in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, including traditional offerings, fasting and community gatherings.
 Chhath Puja in Delhi, Mumbai and Other Indian Cities 
 Migration has helped Chhath Puja become a major public celebration in several Indian cities outside its traditional heartland.
 In Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru and other urban centres, communities arrange temporary ghats and organise collective celebrations.
 In Delhi, devotees gather at designated locations along the Yamuna and at other water bodies. In Mumbai, celebrations take place at approved beaches, lakes and other designated sites, subject to local arrangements.
 These celebrations allow families who have moved away from Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh to continue their traditions.
 Chaiti Chhath: Is Chhath Puja Celebrated Twice a Year? 
 Yes. Chhath Puja is traditionally observed twice a year in many communities.
 The two major observances are:
 1. Kartik Chhath: This is the more widely celebrated observance, held during Kartik Shukla Shashthi in October or November. It is commonly referred to simply as Chhath Puja.
 2. Chaiti Chhath: This observance takes place during Chaitra Shukla Shashthi, generally in March or April. It is observed during the Hindu month of Chaitra and is also dedicated to Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya.
 Kartik Chhath generally attracts larger public participation and is more widely recognised, while Chaiti Chhath is also observed by devotees who follow the tradition.
 The four-day structure and central Sun-worship rituals are similar, although local practices and the scale of celebrations can differ.
 The Environmental Significance of Chhath Puja 
 Chhath Puja has a close relationship with natural elements, particularly the Sun and water.
 The rituals take place near rivers, ponds, lakes and other water bodies. Devotees offer prayers to the Sun while standing in water, and many of the ceremonial offerings are made using locally available fruits, grains and natural materials.
 The festival also encourages communities to clean and prepare the ghats before the celebrations. In many places, residents, volunteers and local authorities work together to make the water bodies and surrounding areas suitable for worship.
 The traditional use of bamboo baskets, earthen lamps and seasonal produce also reflects the festival’s connection with local crafts and agricultural communities.
 However, the environmental benefits of the festival depend on how it is organised. Plastic waste, discarded packaging, food waste and other pollutants can affect rivers and ponds if they are not managed properly.
 Devotees and organisers can help protect water bodies by avoiding single-use plastics, using designated disposal facilities, keeping offerings and packaging out of the water and participating in post-festival clean-up activities.
 The festival’s reverence for the Sun and water provides a meaningful cultural basis for encouraging environmental responsibility.
 Chhath Puja and Agriculture: The Connection with Harvest Traditions 
 Chhath Puja is observed during the post-monsoon period, when many agricultural communities are preparing for or benefiting from seasonal harvests.
 The offerings often include locally available fruits, sugarcane, rice, wheat and other agricultural produce.
 The use of these ingredients reflects the importance of farming and seasonal abundance in the communities where Chhath has long been practised.
 The Sun is essential to agriculture because sunlight supports photosynthesis and influences crop growth. Water, another central element of the festival, is equally important for farming and human life.
 The combination of Sun worship, water-based rituals and agricultural offerings gives Chhath a distinctive connection with the natural resources that sustain communities.
 Chhath Puja Songs: An Important Part of the Celebration 
 Traditional songs are an essential part of Chhath Puja, particularly in Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
 These songs are often sung by women and other family members during preparations, fasting and visits to the ghats.
 They describe the devotion of the vrati, prayers to Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya, family relationships and the importance of the festival.
 Bhojpuri, Maithili and other regional languages are commonly used in Chhath folk songs.
 The songs are passed down through generations and remain an important way of preserving the festival’s cultural heritage.
 Frequently Asked Questions About Chhath Puja 
 When is Chhath Puja in 2026? 
 Chhath Puja 2026 will be observed from November 13 to November 16. The main Sandhya Arghya will take place on November 15, followed by Usha Arghya on November 16. 
 What are the four days of Chhath Puja? 
 The four days are Nahay Khay, Kharna or Lohanda, Sandhya Arghya and Usha Arghya. They involve ritual bathing and food preparation, fasting, evening worship of the setting Sun, and morning worship of the rising Sun. 
 Which God is worshipped during Chhath Puja? 
 Chhath Puja is primarily dedicated to Surya Dev, the Sun God. Devotees also worship Chhathi Maiya, traditionally associated with Shashthi Devi. 
 Why is Chhath Puja celebrated? 
 Chhath Puja is observed to express gratitude to the Sun and seek blessings for health, prosperity, longevity and family well-being. It is also associated with prayers for the protection and happiness of children. 
 Why is the setting Sun worshipped during Chhath? 
 Devotees offer Sandhya Arghya to the setting Sun as an expression of gratitude for the energy and life it provides. The following morning, they offer Usha Arghya to the rising Sun, completing the two-part worship. 
 How long is the Chhath fast? 
 The main Chhath fast is traditionally observed for approximately 36 hours, beginning after the Kharna meal and ending after Usha Arghya on the fourth day. The fast is generally nirjala, meaning devotees abstain from both food and water during this period. 
 What is Nahay Khay? 
 Nahay Khay is the first day of Chhath Puja. Devotees take a ritual bath, clean their homes and prepare a simple meal according to traditional food restrictions. 
 What is Kharna? 
 Kharna is the second day of Chhath Puja. Devotees fast during the day and break the fast after sunset with a traditional offering, commonly rice pudding made with jaggery and accompanied by roti. 
 What is Sandhya Arghya? 
 Sandhya Arghya is the evening offering made to the setting Sun on the third day of Chhath Puja. Devotees gather at water bodies and offer water, fruits and other traditional items. 
 What is Usha Arghya? 
 Usha Arghya is the final major ritual of Chhath Puja. It involves offering prayers and Arghya to the rising Sun on the morning of the fourth day. 
 Why is thekua offered during Chhath Puja? 
 Thekua is a traditional sweet made from wheat flour and jaggery or sugar. It is an important Chhath offering and is distributed as prasad after the rituals. 
 Is Chhath Puja celebrated only in Bihar? 
 No. Although Bihar is one of its most important centres, Chhath is also widely celebrated in Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Nepal and other parts of India. Migrant communities have helped establish celebrations in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata. 
 Is Chhath Puja celebrated twice a year? 
 Yes. The two major observances are Kartik Chhath, celebrated in October or November, and Chaiti Chhath, observed in March or April. 
 Who can observe Chhath Puja? 
 Women and men can observe Chhath Puja. The person undertaking the fast is known as the vrati. Family members and community participants also contribute by preparing offerings and supporting the rituals. 
 Conclusion 
 Chhath Puja is a distinctive Hindu festival that combines devotion to Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya with strict fasting, traditional offerings and community participation. Its four-day observance, from Nahay Khay to Usha Arghya, reflects a deep connection with the Sun, water, family welfare and the natural world.
 Although the festival is especially significant in Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh, its celebrations have spread across India and beyond through communities that continue to preserve its customs.
 From the preparation of thekua and the arrangement of bamboo baskets to the evening offering to the setting Sun and the prayers at sunrise, every part of Chhath carries a distinct cultural and devotional meaning. The festival remains an important expression of faith, gratitude and reverence for the natural forces that sustain life.
